name: Smolov squat program

lead: The Smolov squat routine is a Russian weight-training program named after Sergey Smolov, described as a Master of Sports. It concentrates on the squat, with several heavy sessions per week over a 13-week plan, and is used by lifters who want stronger, bigger legs and glutes.

It was popularised in the West by Pavel Tsatsouline's writing. Reported gains are large, 50 to 130 pounds on the squat according to Wikipedia's summary, but these are anecdotal accounts rather than trial results.

paras: The plan is described in four phases: an introductory phase of squat and lunge variations, a base cycle with four squat sessions a week and a max retest, a switching cycle with negatives and Olympic-style lifts, and an intense mesocycle with three squat sessions a week ending in a strength test. Lifters typically build recovery, food and sleep around it.

High frequency and volume, including back-to-back squat days, make it demanding on joints, the lower back and recovery. Wikipedia notes it is recommended only for elite athletes. Training-injury risk applies, as with any heavy program.

angle.text: Lifters run it to push squat strength up sharply, which they associate with fuller quads and glutes. It is a strength program first; physique change depends on food and recovery around it.

lead: The Smolov squat routine is a 13-week Russian program created by Sergey Smolov to increase squat strength.[1]

Lifters use it as a leg and glute specialisation phase: heavy, frequent squatting builds the quads, glutes and hamstrings, which contribute to a more developed lower body in physique-oriented training. Reported gains for followers are 50 to 130 pounds (22 to 58 kg) on the squat.[1]

The program has four phases: Phase In (two weeks of squat and lunge variations), a four-week Base Cycle with four squat sessions a week and a one-rep max retest, a Switching Cycle of squat negatives and Olympic-style lifts, and an Intense Mesocycle of three squat sessions weekly ending in a final test.[1] It is described as one of the hardest squat routines and was popularised by Pavel Tsatsouline's books.[1]

paras: The routine follows four phases: Phase In, Base Cycle, Switching Cycle and Intense Mesocycle, with retests of the one-rep max at the end of the base and intense phases.[1]
Wikipedia calls it one of the most difficult squat routines around and notes its three to four training days per week, some on consecutive days, and its recommendation for elite athletes only.[1]
